title: Conversational Agents in Health Care: Scoping Review and Conceptual Analysis
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly growing use of conversational agents (chatbots and similar dialogue systems) in health care, asking what kinds of systems have been studied, how they are used, and what evidence exists regarding their accuracy, acceptability, and effectiveness. The authors note that the field was fragmented, descriptive, and lacked a clear overview of applications and evaluation approaches.

The paper is a scoping review and conceptual analysis of literature published up to April 2019. The authors searched major biomedical databases and gray literature sources, ultimately including 47 study reports (45 studies and 2 ongoing trials). Because the review is about health care rather than education, there is no teacher, student, or school-based intervention context. The included studies covered a range of health applications, such as treatment and monitoring, service support, education, lifestyle behavior change, and diagnosis, with most systems delivered through smartphone apps and often using text-based interaction.

Across the included studies, the review found that conversational agents were usually evaluated through case studies, surveys, or randomized controlled trials, with generally positive findings for accuracy, acceptability, and effectiveness. However, the evidence base was dominated by small, descriptive studies, with limited reporting on adverse effects, cost, and implementation in real-world health systems. The authors conclude that more robust evaluations are needed, especially for safety, effectiveness, and integration into existing services.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Conversational agents or chatbots that simulate human text or voice conversations using rules-based or machine-learning/NLP methods.
identified_tools.use_case: This scoping review examined health care conversational agents in general, including their applications, characteristics, and evaluation across the literature, rather than one specific product.

findings.finding_summary: The review identified 47 study reports (45 studies and 2 ongoing clinical trials) on health care conversational agents. The literature was largely descriptive, with most agents delivered via smartphone apps, using free-text input/output, and only 11 randomized controlled trials; the authors concluded there is an urgent need for more robust evaluation focused on acceptability, safety, and effectiveness.
findings.measure: Study characteristics and evaluation outcomes across included literature
findings.sample_size: n=47 study reports (45 studies, 2 ongoing clinical trials)

quality_tier_rationale: This is a scoping review, not an empirical evaluation of a single AI tool. It synthesizes heterogeneous conversational-agent studies and does not provide a rigorous causal estimate for one product.
impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests broad use and generally positive evaluations across health care conversational agents, but it does not report a pooled effect size or a clear measured impact for one tool. The evidence is therefore informative but not directly quantifiable for impact.
